title: Chicago Gloves and Illinois Mats
bigQuestion: How did newspapers, park districts and a state school association build rooms for combat sports in Chicago and Illinois?

story.title: One Glass Case, Two Rule Books
story.kicker: A wrestling bracket and a Golden Gloves program sit side by side behind the same glass.
paragraphs: A Chicago high school has a long glass trophy case outside its gym. Most shelves hold basketball and track trophies. On the bottom shelf sit two faded pieces of paper. One is a state wrestling bracket from the IHSA finals. The other is a program from the Chicago Golden Gloves boxing tournament.

A student named Darius stops to look during passing period. The bracket has lines that join names, round by round, down to one champion at each weight. One name is circled in pen. It belongs to a wrestler who graduated from the school decades ago.

The Golden Gloves program is thinner. Its cover shows a small gold boxing glove. Inside are lists of boxers by weight class, with the names of the parks and gyms they trained in. One of those names is the same field house where Darius plays basketball on Saturdays.

Darius's history teacher walks by and sees him reading. "Those two papers came from two different rule books," she says. "One tournament was run by a state association of schools. The other was started with help from a newspaper." Darius looks again at the gold glove.
story.think: Why would a school keep papers from two different sports and two different organizations in the same case?

lessons.title: Gloves Made of Gold
lessons.mainIdea: The Golden Gloves is an amateur boxing tournament that big-city newspapers helped start in the late 1920s.
reading: The *Golden Gloves* is a tournament for amateur boxers. The New York Daily News ran a Golden Gloves tournament starting in 1927. By the late 1920s, the Chicago Tribune ran a Golden Gloves tournament in Chicago as well. Both papers printed the entry forms, the brackets and the results.

A champion in each weight class wins a small gold charm shaped like a boxing glove. That prize gave the tournament its name. Boxers are grouped by weight so that each match pairs people of similar size. Many local tournaments also split entrants into *novice* and open divisions, so beginners meet other beginners.

The Golden Gloves drew young boxers from Chicago's neighborhoods, parks and settlement houses. It was a way to compete in a large arena without turning professional. Winners in Chicago could go on to meet winners from other cities. The tournament still runs in Chicago today.

words.d: an amateur boxing tournament started with newspaper support in the late 1920s; champions win a small gold glove
a beginner; in boxing, a division for boxers with few past bouts

look.title: A Program Page
look.text: A page from an old Golden Gloves program lists boxers under headings by weight. Next to each name is a park, a gym or a club. A box at the bottom lists the tournament rules: amateur boxers only, and every boxer weighs in on the day of the bout.
look.prompt: What can a historian learn about a city's neighborhoods from the names of the gyms and parks on this page?

check.q: Which Chicago newspaper ran the city's Golden Gloves tournament?
check.why: The Chicago Tribune ran the Chicago Golden Gloves; the New York Daily News ran New York's.

check.q: What is a novice division?
choices: a division for the heaviest boxers
a division for boxers with few past bouts
check.why: A novice division lets beginners meet other beginners.

lessons.title: A Newspaper as Promoter
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago Tribune sports editor Arch Ward used his paper to build big public sports events, including the first baseball All-Star Game.
reading: In the early 1900s, newspapers were a main source of sports news. A paper that ran its own event could fill its sports pages for weeks. It could also sell more copies. A *promoter* is a person or group that organizes an event and draws a crowd to it.

*Arch Ward* became sports editor of the Chicago Tribune in 1930 and held the job until his death in 1955. He backed the Tribune's Golden Gloves. In 1933 he created baseball's first All-Star Game, played at Comiskey Park during Chicago's Century of Progress world's fair.

In 1934, Ward started the College All-Star Game in football, played at Soldier Field. Both games drew large crowds and weeks of Tribune stories. Ward showed that a newspaper could be more than a reporter of sports. It could also be the organizer.

words.d: a person or group that organizes an event and draws a crowd to it
Chicago Tribune sports editor from 1930 to 1955 who organized big public sports events

look.title: Reporter and Organizer
look.text: Imagine the Tribune sports page in the week of the Golden Gloves finals. It prints the bracket, photos of the boxers, the ticket prices and a story praising the tournament. The paper is also the group running the tournament.
look.prompt: What might be good about a newspaper running an event? What might be a problem when it also reports on that event?

choices: a person or group that organizes an event and draws a crowd

check.why: A promoter organizes an event and draws people to it.

check.q: What event did Arch Ward create in 1933?
check.why: Ward created baseball's first All-Star Game, played at Comiskey Park in 1933.

check.q: Why did newspapers like the Tribune run their own sports events?
choices: to fill their sports pages and sell more copies
check.why: An event the paper ran gave it weeks of stories and helped sell papers.

lessons.title: From City Ring to Olympic Ring
lessons.mainIdea: Amateur tournaments like the Golden Gloves fed a path that led toward national titles and the Olympic Games.
reading: Boxing first appeared at the modern Olympics in 1904, at St. Louis, Missouri. Only American boxers entered that year. Olympic boxing has been for amateurs for most of its history. That made amateur tournaments the first step toward an Olympic team.

By the 1930s, Golden Gloves champions from Chicago and New York met each year in an *Intercity* tournament. Later, a national Golden Gloves tournament brought together champions from many cities. A local win could lead to a national title and to Olympic trials.

For decades, the Amateur Athletic Union, or AAU, governed many U.S. amateur sports, including boxing. The *Amateur Sports Act of 1978* changed that. It required each Olympic sport to have its own national governing body. For amateur boxing, that body is now USA Boxing.

words.d: a Golden Gloves tournament between champions of Chicago and New York
a U.S. law that gave each Olympic sport its own national governing body

check.why: Boxing first appeared at the 1904 Olympics in St. Louis, Missouri.

check.why: Intercity matches paired Golden Gloves champions from Chicago and New York.

lessons.title: Field Houses for Neighborhoods
lessons.mainIdea: In 1905, Chicago's South Park Commission opened neighborhood parks with field houses that gave crowded areas indoor public rooms.
reading: In the early 1900s, many Chicago workers lived in crowded neighborhoods near the stockyards, rail yards and factories. Few homes had space for sports. Reformers argued that small parks close to homes would help families. In 1905, the South Park Commission opened a set of new neighborhood parks on the South Side.

Each new park had a *field house*, a public building for indoor activities. The field houses were designed by the firm of D. H. Burnham and Company. The Olmsted Brothers firm designed the grounds. Inside were gymnasiums, locker rooms, showers, club rooms and, in many, a branch of the Chicago Public Library.

A field house gym was a public room. Anyone in the neighborhood could use it, not only those who paid tuition. Over the century, these rooms hosted basketball, dances, meetings, and boxing and martial arts classes. Several field houses from 1905 still stand and are city landmarks.

words.d: a public park building with a gym and rooms for indoor activities
the board that ran parks on Chicago's South Side before 1934

look.prompt: Who might walk through each door? What paid for each room?

check.q: When did the South Park Commission open its new neighborhood parks?
check.why: The South Park Commission opened its new neighborhood parks with field houses in 1905.

check.q: Which firm designed the 1905 field houses?
check.why: D. H. Burnham and Company designed the buildings; the Olmsted Brothers designed the grounds.

lessons.title: One Park District
lessons.mainIdea: In 1934, Chicago joined its separate park boards into one Chicago Park District, which still runs public rooms across the city.
reading: Before 1934, Chicago had 22 separate park districts. Each had its own board, taxes and staff. The Great Depression made it hard for the small districts to pay their debts. Voters approved joining them into one body, the *Chicago Park District*, in 1934.

The new district took over parks, beaches, field houses and Soldier Field. Today it runs hundreds of parks across the city. It is a unit of local *government*, with a board and a budget funded mostly by property taxes. Its programs are open to all city residents.

Park district rooms have hosted boxing for generations. Programs at some field houses train young boxers who enter the Chicago Golden Gloves. Other parks offer martial arts classes. A park district class can reach children whose families could not pay storefront tuition.

words.d: the city park agency formed in 1934 by joining 22 separate park districts
the public bodies that make laws, collect taxes and run services

look.title: One Agency for One City
look.text: Before 1934, a family on the North Side and a family on the South Side paid taxes to different park boards. Each board had its own staff and its own debts. After 1934, one Chicago Park District board set programs and budgets for parks across the whole city.
look.prompt: Why might one citywide park agency be easier to run than 22 small ones?

check.q: How many park districts were joined to form the Chicago Park District?
check.why: Chicago's 22 separate park districts were joined in 1934.

check.q: What problem helped push Chicago to join its park districts in 1934?
choices: the Great Depression made debts hard to pay
check.why: During the Great Depression the small districts struggled to pay their debts.

check.q: How can a park district boxing class help a family?
choices: It can cost less than storefront tuition because taxes help pay for it
It is run by a newspaper
check.why: Park programs are funded mostly by taxes, so they can charge low fees.

lessons.title: A Settlement Gym and a Stadium
lessons.mainIdea: Hull-House and Soldier Field show two kinds of Chicago rooms: a neighborhood gym and a giant public stadium.
reading: Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr opened *Hull-House* on Halsted Street in 1889. It was a *settlement house*, a center where reformers lived among immigrant neighbors and offered classes and services. The Near West Side around it was home to Italian, Greek, Jewish and many other families. In the 1890s, Hull-House added a gymnasium.

Soldier Field opened in 1924 on the lakefront. On September 22, 1927, it held the heavyweight rematch between Gene Tunney and Jack Dempsey. More than 100,000 people came. Tunney won by decision, and the bout is remembered for the "long count" after a knockdown in the seventh round.

The two rooms show two sides of the city's combat sports. A settlement gym gave neighbors a free, small space to exercise and learn. A stadium sold tickets to a huge crowd to watch two professionals. Both were Chicago public history.

words.d: the settlement house founded by Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr in Chicago in 1889
a neighborhood center where reformers lived and offered classes and services to immigrants

check.why: Settlement houses like Hull-House offered classes and services to immigrant neighbors.

lessons.title: An Association of Schools
lessons.mainIdea: The IHSA, founded in 1900, runs Illinois high school state tournaments, and Illinois helped found the national NFHS in 1920.
reading: The *Illinois High School Association*, or IHSA, was founded in 1900. Its headquarters is in Bloomington, Illinois. It is an association of member high schools. The schools agree on eligibility rules, such as grades and age, and the IHSA runs the state tournaments.

In 1920, leaders from Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Michigan and Wisconsin met in Chicago. They formed the Midwest Federation of State High School Athletic Associations. It grew into the national NFHS, which moved its headquarters to Indianapolis. Illinois was one of its five founding states.

The NFHS writes national rule books for many high school sports, including wrestling. The IHSA uses those rules and adds its own for Illinois, such as how schools are split into classes by enrollment. An *association* is a group whose members join together to make shared rules.

words.d: the IHSA; founded in 1900, it runs Illinois high school state tournaments
a group whose members join together to make shared rules
the rules about who is allowed to compete, such as grades and age

look.prompt: Why does the coach need both books? What does each one decide?

check.why: Leaders from Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Michigan and Wisconsin met in Chicago in 1920.

check.why: Eligibility rules decide who is allowed to compete.

lessons.title: Boys' State Finals Since 1937
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois boys have wrestled for IHSA state titles since 1937, through a series of tournaments that ends in a state final bracket.
reading: The IHSA crowned its first boys state wrestling champions in 1937. That was more than 35 years after the IHSA began. Each season ends with a *state series*: regional tournaments, then sectionals, then the state finals. Wrestlers who place high enough move on to the next round.

At each level, wrestlers are listed on a *bracket*, a chart that pairs them and shows who advances. Each weight class has its own bracket. The IHSA also splits schools into classes by enrollment, so small schools compete with small schools and large schools with large schools.

For many years, the individual state finals have been held at the University of Illinois arena in Champaign. The IHSA keeps a record book with every state champion by year, weight and school. That book is a primary source for the history of Illinois wrestling.

words.d: the chain of tournaments, from regionals to state finals, that decides state champions
a chart that pairs competitors and shows who moves on
a record made at the time, such as a bracket, program or record book

check.why: A record made at the time, like a list of champions, is a primary source.

lessons.title: Girls Get Their Own Bracket
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois held its first girls state wrestling finals in 2022, fifty years after Title IX barred sex discrimination in school programs.
reading: In 1972, Congress passed *Title IX* of the Education Amendments. It bans discrimination based on sex in any education program that gets federal money. High school sports count as education programs. Title IX opened many girls teams across the country.

Combat sports moved slowly. For decades, girls who wanted to wrestle in Illinois high schools joined boys teams and wrestled boys. Their numbers grew over many years. Other states started separate girls tournaments before Illinois did.

The IHSA held its first girls state wrestling finals in 2022, at the end of the 2021–22 season. Girls now have their own weight classes and their own state bracket. The first girls champions joined the IHSA record book, eighty-five years after the first boys champions.

words.d: a 1972 U.S. law that bans sex discrimination in education programs that get federal money
treating people unfairly because of who they are, such as their sex or race

look.title: The Words of Title IX
look.text: No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.
look.cite: Title IX, Education Amendments of 1972, 20 U.S.C. § 1681
look.prompt: Which words in the law could a girl use to ask for a place on a school team?

check.q: When did Congress pass Title IX?
check.why: Title IX is part of the Education Amendments of 1972.

choices: They could not wrestle at all by law
They joined boys teams and wrestled boys
They wrestled only in Golden Gloves
check.why: Girls joined boys teams and wrestled boys until the IHSA added girls state finals.

check.q: How many years passed between the first IHSA boys and girls wrestling champions?
check.why: The first boys champions were crowned in 1937 and the first girls champions in 2022: 85 years.

lessons.title: Many Rule Books, One Case
lessons.mainIdea: Each trophy in a school case was won under a different rule book written by a different body.
reading: A school trophy case looks like one collection. Each object in it, though, comes from its own set of rules. A wrestling plaque was won under the NFHS rule book, in a state series run by the IHSA. A basketball trophy was also won under NFHS rules, but in a different sport with different officials.

A Golden Gloves program comes from outside the school. The bouts followed amateur boxing rules set by USA Boxing and the tournament's organizers. A judo medal from a local tournament followed rules shaped by the International Judo Federation. The school simply chose to display it.

Historians call an object like a trophy or program an *artifact*. An artifact is made by people and survives from the past. Reading an artifact means asking who made it, under what rules, and for whom. A single glass case can hold artifacts from four or five different governing bodies.

words.d: an object made by people that survives from the past
to show objects so that people can see them, as in a trophy case

look.title: Labels in the Case

look.prompt: For each object, which organization's rules do you think it was won under?

choices: an object made by people that survives from the past
check.why: An artifact is a human-made object from the past, such as a trophy or program.

check.q: Which body writes the rules a high school wrestling plaque was won under?
check.why: High school wrestling follows the NFHS rule book, with the IHSA running the state series.

check.q: What rules did bouts in a Golden Gloves tournament follow?
check.why: Golden Gloves bouts follow amateur boxing rules.

lessons.title: Records That Keep Names
lessons.mainIdea: Record books, brackets and programs keep the names of athletes and let historians trace who could compete and when.
reading: Each organization keeps its own *records*. The IHSA lists state wrestling champions by year and school. Golden Gloves programs and newspaper pages list boxers by weight and gym. These papers survive in school offices, family boxes and library *archives*.

Historians use such records to answer questions. When do girls' names first appear in state results? Which neighborhoods sent boxers to the Golden Gloves in the 1930s? Which schools won titles in the first years after 1937? Each answer depends on a record kept at the time.

Records also show gaps. A list of champions from 1937 to 2021 has no girls bracket, because none existed. A missing name can be as important as a printed one. Reading records carefully helps explain whose stories were saved and whose were left out.

words.d: written lists or papers kept by an organization, such as champions by year
places where old records and papers are kept for study

check.q: What is an archive?
choices: a place where old records are kept for study
check.why: An archive keeps old records and papers so people can study them.
